scope_summary: Prime coat application for bare drywall ceiling surfaces in new construction. Single prime coat (no finish coats). Assumes drywall is taped, mudded, and sanded by drywall contractor prior to painting scope. Covers flat ceilings, tray ceiling flat areas, and vaulted/cathedral ceiling areas. Does NOT include wall prime, ceiling finish coats, wood/beadboard ceilings, or coffered ceiling beams.
relevant_findings: PVA (polyvinyl acetate) primer is the standard choice for new drywall ceilings — same material systems as wall prime
Ceiling priming is typically done at the same time as wall priming in NC sequence, but overhead application is distinctly slower
Spray+backroll is the most common production method for ceilings in NC — spray-only is less common because backroll ensures consolidation on overhead surfaces
Single primer coat is standard — ceilings have the same drywall absorption characteristics as walls
New construction drywall fasteners are mudded and rust-resistant — no spot-priming needed (inherits RC-001 from wall prime)
PVA and acrylic primers are sealers, not stain blockers — zero stain blocking (inherits RC-002 from wall prime)
Overhead work is physically more demanding and slower than wall work — production rates are 15-25% lower than equivalent wall prime rates
Height modifiers are more aggressive for ceilings: standard 8-9ft ceiling is baseline, but vaulted (13-17ft) and cathedral (18ft+) require scaffolding/lifts and significantly reduce throughput
Floor protection is ALWAYS required for ceiling spray work — full room coverage (floor_full), not perimeter only
Wall protection during ceiling spray depends on NC sequence — if walls are not yet painted (typical), wall masking may not be needed; if walls are finished, wall_adjacent protection applies
Drywall dust on ceilings is the same concern as walls — must vacuum before priming for proper adhesion
Ceiling edge cut-in at wall line is the inverse of wall cut-in at ceiling line — same physical edge, different perspective

prep_requirements.method: HEPA vacuum with brush attachment — overhead technique
prep_requirements.reason: Drywall dust reduces adhesion and causes visible contamination in primer film. Gravity means less dust accumulation on ceilings than walls, but still critical.

prep_requirements.method: Walk with work light (angled to reveal defects), mark defects
prep_requirements.reason: Identify fastener pops, unfilled joints, damaged paper. Lighting angle is critical for ceiling inspection — direct overhead light hides defects that raking light reveals.
prep_requirements.skip_conditions: QT2 may reduce to major defects only

limitations: Zero stain blocking — sealer only, not a stain blocker (RC-002)

advantages: Better adhesion and build than PVA

ceiling_specific_considerations.impact: All ceiling tasks take longer than equivalent wall tasks due to overhead body position. Fatigue compounds over time — production rates decrease through the workday for ceiling work more than wall work.
Standard 8-9ft ceilings: work from floor with extension pole. 10-12ft: step ladder may be needed. 13-17ft vaulted: scaffold or baker staging. 18ft+ cathedral: scaffold, possibly lifts.
ceiling_specific_considerations.rate_adjustment: Height modifiers per Estimation_Modifiers_Doctrine: H1=1.0, H2=1.3, H3=1.5, H4=2.0

ceiling_specific_considerations.impact: Ceiling spray requires different technique than walls — sprayer aims upward, overspray falls straight down onto operator and floor. Full PPE more critical. Spray fan angle and distance differ.
ceiling_specific_considerations.rate_adjustment: Ceiling spray rate ~15% slower than wall spray rate

ceiling_specific_considerations.impact: Backrolling a ceiling is done with extension pole at arm's length overhead. Significantly more fatiguing than wall backroll. Roller control is harder — more drips and stipple risk.
ceiling_specific_considerations.rate_adjustment: Ceiling backroll rate ~20% slower than wall backroll rate

ceiling_specific_considerations.impact: Ceiling spray creates overspray that falls to the floor across the entire room. Floor protection must be full room (floor_full zone), not just perimeter. This is mandatory regardless of floor type.
ceiling_specific_considerations.rate_adjustment: Protection setup time is higher than wall spray protection

required_paintscope_keys.required_when: Always — primary quantity driver for ceiling priming

required_paintscope_keys.description: Linear footage of ceiling-to-wall boundary for edge cut-in from the ceiling's perspective. Distinct key from wall's PS_EDGE_LF.TO_CEILING — each surface declares its own edge relationship.
required_paintscope_keys.required_when: When application_method is roll, or when spray requires edge touch-up at wall line

paintscope_key_resolution.resolution: Created PS_EDGE_LF.TO_WALL as a distinct key. Each surface declares its own edge relationship — wall uses PS_EDGE_LF.TO_CEILING, ceiling uses PS_EDGE_LF.TO_WALL.
paintscope_key_resolution.rationale: Same physical edge but each spec declares its own PaintScope key. This maintains clear ownership: wall specs reference TO_CEILING, ceiling specs reference TO_WALL. PaintScope resolves both from the same measured geometry.

zones_required.rationale: Ceiling spray creates overspray that falls to floor across entire room. Full floor coverage mandatory.
Roll method has minimal drip risk — perimeter drops sufficient.
If walls have been painted (atypical NC sequence), wall drapes needed during ceiling spray. If walls are bare (typical NC), no wall protection needed.
Any fixtures installed before priming need protection from overspray.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: Ceiling and walls are almost always different products (primer vs finish, or different colors). Edge work at this boundary is the primary adjacency concern.
adjacent_surfaces.affected_tasks: Cut-in at wall line, masking at wall line

adjacent_surfaces.notes: Crown molding, if present, creates a ceiling-to-trim boundary. In NC sequence, crown is typically installed after ceiling prime, so this edge is not relevant during prime phase. Included for completeness — affects ceiling finish spec more than prime.

conditions_affecting_tasks.impact: Floor protection material selection: rosin paper on hard floors, canvas/plastic on carpet. Subfloor may not require protection.
Ceiling height determines access equipment. Standard ceilings = none/step_ladder. Vaulted = scaffold. Cathedral = scaffold/lift.
conditions_affecting_tasks.affects_tasks: All ceiling application tasks — production rate modifiers

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: May require brush cut-in if walls are on separate phase or different product. In NC, walls and ceilings are often primed in same session — edge work may be minimal.
adjacency_notes.nc_context: In NC, ceilings are typically primed at the same time as walls. Ceiling primer should stop at wall line without extending onto wall surface.

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: Crown molding is typically NOT installed during prime phase in NC. If pre-installed (rare), creates masking requirement.
adjacency_notes.nc_context: Crown molding installed after prime, before finish. Not a prime-phase concern.

notes_for_materials_manager: Same material systems as wall prime — PVA for QT2-QT3, acrylic latex for QT4, high-build for Level 5
Coverage rates are the same as wall prime (same drywall substrate, same absorption)
Ceiling spray may use slightly higher product volume due to overspray losses overhead
Spray tip selection same as walls — 517 standard
Roller nap selection same as walls — 1/2" smooth, 3/4" textured
Floor protection materials are higher quantity than wall prime — full room coverage needed for spray
notes_for_sop_librarian: Mirror wall prime SOP structure with ceiling-specific task IDs (TSK_CEIL_* prefix)
Vacuum step is CRITICAL — same as walls (RC-001 applies: no spot-priming of fasteners)
Spray+backroll coupling constraint same as walls — backroller sets pace
Edge cut-in is at WALL line (not ceiling line) — inverse of wall spec
Floor protection is full-room for spray methods (not perimeter)
Wall protection is conditional on NC sequence — typically NOT needed during prime phase
Masking scope is different from wall prime: mask wall tops (not ceiling line), mask floor fully
notes_for_estimation_engineer: All production rates should be 15-25% slower than wall prime equivalents due to overhead work
Roll rates: ~300 SF/hr smooth ceiling (vs 350 wall), ~235 SF/hr textured (vs 275 wall)
Backroll rates: ~325 SF/hr ceiling (vs 400 wall) — overhead fatigue is significant
Effective spray+backroll rate = backroll rate (coupling constraint, same as walls)
Cut-in rates: ~85 LF/hr ceiling edge (vs 100 wall) — working overhead
Height modifiers per Modifier_Registry: H1=1.0 (≤9ft), H2=1.3 (10-12ft), H3=1.5 (13-17ft), H4=2.0 (18ft+)
Height modifiers compound with the inherent overhead slowdown — a cathedral ceiling is both overhead AND high access
QT modifiers same as walls: QT2=0.8, QT3=1.0, QT4=1.3
Floor protection setup is larger scope than wall spray — budget more protection time
assumptions: All drywall is standard gypsum board (not specialized types)
New construction surface condition is 'Good' — minimal defects expected
Standard ceiling height 8-9 ft is baseline; height modifiers apply above that
Drywall contractor has completed all taping, mudding, and sanding
Ceilings and walls are typically primed in the same session in NC production
Floor protection is always needed for ceiling spray — no exceptions
Crown molding is NOT installed during prime phase (typical NC sequence)
uncertainties: Exact overhead fatigue factor for ceiling work — 15-25% range needs field validation
Whether ceiling spray+backroll rate reduction is closer to 15% or 25% vs walls
Floor condition at time of ceiling prime — site_condition_rules handle this
Whether wall protection is ever needed during ceiling prime in NC sequence — treated as conditional

inherited_research_corrections.title: No spot-priming NC drywall fasteners
inherited_research_corrections.impact: No spot-prime tasks in ceiling spec — same reasoning as wall prime

inherited_research_corrections.title: PVA/acrylic drywall primers have zero stain blocking
inherited_research_corrections.impact: No stain blocking claims in materials — same reasoning as wall prime

inherited_research_corrections.title: Floor protection conditional on floor_type
inherited_research_corrections.impact: Site condition rules for floor_type apply — but ceiling spray always requires floor_full regardless

inherited_research_corrections.title: Do not specify dry times in specs
inherited_research_corrections.impact: No dry time references in ceiling spec
